title: 8085 assembly programming
subtitle: Write it, assemble it, single-step it. Every program below runs in the simulator with real opcodes, flags and T-states.

sections.title: Your first program: add two numbers
sections.body:
Time to make the chip do something. Your first program adds two numbers, and you can run it right now. Memory holds 25H at 2050H and 17H at 2051H. You load HL with the address, fetch the first byte into A, step to the next, add it, step on, and store. The result is 3CH at 2052H (25H + 17H = 3CH), and since nothing overflowed, CY = 0.

Watch HL walk along memory in the figure. And why INX H between the reads? To move the pointer from the first byte to the second one.

questions.prompt: Why INX H between the reads?

choices.text: To advance the memory pointer HL to the next byte.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: MOV A,M and ADD M always use the address in HL.

figures.caption: Figure 2.7.1 — add two bytes
figures.script:
var lab = create("steplab", {"name":"add","engine":"cpu8085","program":"LXI H,2050H
MOV A,M
INX H
ADD M
INX H
MOV M,A
HLT","memory":"2050=25,17","watch":"2050,2051,2052","width":600,"height":440});

keynotes: Memory holds 25H at 2050H and 17H at 2051H; HL points to the data, A takes the first byte and the second is added.
The result 3CH is stored at 2052H and CY = 0.
INX H moves the pointer to the next byte between the reads.

sections.title: Loops and conditions
sections.body:
Computers shine at repetition, and a loop is simply a counter, a body and a conditional jump back. Let’s sum 5+4+3+2+1: B counts down, A accumulates, and JNZ LOOP repeats while the zero flag is clear. The result is 0FH (15), and on exit Z = 1.

Unroll it to see the arithmetic: A = 0, then add B = 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, so 0 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15 = 0FH. In the figure, DCR sets Z when B reaches 0, and JNZ then falls through. JNZ LOOP jumps when the zero flag is not set, so while B has not reached zero.

worked.why: Unroll the loop: A = 0, then add B = 5, 4, 3, 2, 1.

choices.text: The zero flag is 0 (last result was not zero).

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: So the loop ends when DCR makes B zero.

figures.caption: Figure 2.8.1 — sum 1 to 5
figures.note: DCR sets Z when B reaches 0; JNZ then falls through.
figures.script:
var lab = create("steplab", {"name":"loop","engine":"cpu8085","program":"MVI B,5
MVI A,0
LOOP: ADD B
DCR B
JNZ LOOP
HLT","memory":"","watch":"","width":600,"height":440});

keynotes: A loop is a counter, a body and a conditional jump back.
Summing 5+4+3+2+1 with B counting down, A accumulating and JNZ LOOP gives 0FH (15), and on exit Z = 1.
JNZ jumps while the zero flag is clear.

sections.title: Comparison and branching
sections.body:
How does a processor decide anything? It sets flags, then jumps. That is the whole of decision-making. CMP r compares A with r without changing A: Z = 1 if equal, CY = 1 if A < r.

Use it to find the larger of two numbers. This program stores the larger of 25H and 17H at 2052H, which is 25H. As the figure says, CMP sets carry when A < B. So after CMP B, CY = 1 exactly when A is less than B. Remember the pattern: set flags, then conditional jump.

questions.prompt: After CMP B, when is CY = 1?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The internal subtraction needed a borrow.

figures.caption: Figure 2.9.1 — the larger of two
figures.note: CMP sets carry when A < B.
figures.script:
var lab = create("steplab", {"name":"max","engine":"cpu8085","program":"LDA 2050H
MOV B,A
LDA 2051H
CMP B
JNC DONE
MOV A,B
DONE: STA 2052H
HLT","memory":"2050=25,17","watch":"2050,2051,2052","width":600,"height":440});

keynotes: CMP r compares A with r without changing A: Z = 1 if equal, CY = 1 if A < r.
The example stores the larger of 25H and 17H, which is 25H, at 2052H.
Decision-making is always set flags, then conditional jump.

sections.title: Arrays and table processing
sections.body: Real data comes in blocks, and the pattern for handling them is one you will use for life: pointer, counter, loop. Sum four bytes at 2050H–2053H: HL points to the array, C counts four, A accumulates. The result is 0AH at 2060H (1+2+3+4 = 10 = 0AH). Four passes through the loop, as the figure shows. In the array loop, it is INX H that moves the pointer along; this pattern handles any block.

questions.prompt: In the array loop, what moves the pointer?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: HL advances one byte per pass.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: That adds the byte; it does not move HL.

figures.caption: Figure 2.10.1 — sum a table
figures.script:
var lab = create("steplab", {"name":"arr","engine":"cpu8085","program":"LXI H,2050H
MVI C,04H
MVI A,00H
NEXT: ADD M
INX H
DCR C
JNZ NEXT
STA 2060H
HLT","memory":"2050=01,02,03,04","watch":"2050,2051,2052,2053,2060","width":600,"height":440});

keynotes: Sum four bytes at 2050H–2053H: HL points to the array, C counts four and A accumulates.
The pattern pointer + counter + loop handles any block.

sections.title: BCD arithmetic and DAA
sections.body:
Here is a puzzle: add 38 and 45 on a binary machine and you do not get 83. In BCD each decimal digit occupies a nibble. Adding 38H and 45H in plain binary gives 7DH, not the BCD 83. The fix is the instruction DAA (decimal adjust accumulator): it adds 6 to a nibble above 9 or with auxiliary carry. Here 38H + 45H = 7DH → DAA → 83H (= 83 decimal).

Step past ADI and again past DAA in the figure and watch the accumulator change. So DAA turns a binary sum of BCD digits into a correct BCD result.

choices.text: Corrects the accumulator after a binary addition of BCD digits.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It adds 6 to any nibble greater than 9.

figures.caption: Figure 2.11.1 — BCD addition
figures.note: Step past ADI and again past DAA.

problems.prompt: Add 99 and 01 in BCD on the 8085. What are A and CY afterwards?
problems.answer: Binary: 99H + 01H = 9AH. DAA adds 66H → 00H with a carry out: A = 00H, CY = 1 (the decimal 100).

keynotes: In BCD each decimal digit occupies a nibble.
Adding 38 and 45 in plain binary gives 7DH, not the BCD 83.
DAA adds 6 to a nibble above 9 or with auxiliary carry, so 38H + 45H = 7DH becomes 83H.

sections.title: Subroutines and the stack
sections.body:
Good programs are built from reusable pieces, called subroutines. CALL pushes the return address on the stack (SP decreases by 2) and jumps; RET pops it. Always initialise SP first (LXI SP,…), or the return address will land somewhere you did not intend. PUSH and POP save registers around a call. The stack grows downward in memory.

In the figure you can see that after CALL, SP has dropped by 2, and after RET it is restored. After CALL, then, the stack pointer is lower by 2 than before.

choices.text: Decreases by 2 (the return address is pushed).

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The 8085 stack grows toward lower addresses.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: The return address is stored there.

figures.caption: Figure 2.12.1 — call and return
figures.note: After CALL, SP has dropped by 2; after RET it is restored.
figures.script:
var lab = create("steplab", {"name":"call","engine":"cpu8085","program":"LXI SP,3000H
MVI A,7
CALL DBL
HLT
DBL: ADD A
RET","memory":"","watch":"","width":600,"height":440});

keynotes: CALL pushes the return address on the stack (SP decreases by 2) and jumps; RET pops it.
Always initialise SP first (LXI SP,…); PUSH and POP save registers around a call.
The stack grows downward in memory.
